question: Should OpenClaw adopt the RFC's generic recursive path-authority model as the permanent core configuration contract, or solve managed deployment ownership through a narrower extension of the existing `$include` and fail-closed write-through model?
rationale: Both approaches can address the Lobster use case, but they create materially different long-term configuration APIs, compatibility obligations, and authorization boundaries that automation cannot choose safely.

options.title: Continue generic RFC review
options.body: Keep the draft open and settle source identity, mutation, comparator, rollback, and upgrade semantics with live lifecycle proof.

options.title: Narrow the design
options.body: Revise the RFC around bounded managed paths or include ownership while preserving existing config behavior by default.

options.title: Keep overlays host-owned
options.body: Decline a core authority contract and retain deployment-specific overlay machinery outside OpenClaw.

recommendation.title: Continue generic RFC review
recommendation.body: Keep the draft open and settle source identity, mutation, comparator, rollback, and upgrade semantics with live lifecycle proof.

likelyOwner.reason: @steipete introduced the closest current config write-through contract and is the strongest history-based owner for deciding whether to generalize it.
